Adaptive task resources

Settings → Autonomous resources controls the project-local resource_policy in config/manager.json. Save does not start a provider or queue. Existing projects retain their old behavior until the policy is enabled. Policy changes wait for an active queue to finish; restarting a server is not a way to change the allowance of an already running session.

The default session count is editable independently of automatic estimation. With adaptive budgets enabled, the initial estimate is 3 sessions for a small routine task, the configured default for standard work, default + 4 for complex work, and default + 8 for critical work. A review rejection adds room for repair. The run allowance, overall time limit, and automatic per-task ceiling still apply. Estimates count all lifecycle roles, including review and verification. Unused sessions are an allowance, not work ATL must perform.

Only allocations marked source: automatic may grow automatically. With automatic extension enabled, the manager can reserve the remaining lifecycle handoffs at each session boundary, up to the ceiling. It never resets used. Legacy task limits and owner increases are pinned; changing a Settings default does not override them. An explicit run session limit can impose a lower cap. When extension is disabled, the first automatic allocation remains fixed.

Model routing uses an owner-approved pool of exact provider/model pairs. Each pair has an economy, standard, or advanced capability tier, an enabled flag, and a cost order from 0 to 100. Cost order is a relative owner preference, not a price quotation. The strongest allowed tier and enabled rows together define the ceiling. Adding a provider connection does not automatically enroll its models. Installed model metadata supplies input suggestions; availability in a local catalog is not a guarantee of account entitlement or runtime success.

Before each role session, ATL estimates required capacity from the task's own scope, files, dependencies, risk, acceptance surfaces and review results. A planner can supply a reasoned resource_estimate; it cannot downgrade observed risk, choose an unauthorized provider, or increase a ceiling. Genuine review rejections increase required reasoning capacity; risky independent reviews use the advanced tier. The lowest configured cost order among available models meeting the requirement wins. This is an inspectable bounded routing rule, not a learned price or performance predictor.

Completed and independently verified execution histories now calibrate future session estimates and model tier requirements within the same owner bounds. See Execution reports for coverage, cohort thresholds and the distinction between runtime adaptation and model weight training.

Explicit role or run selections are preserved and validated against the same pool, capacity requirement and ceiling. An unavailable or inadequate route stops before starting or charging a model session and names what is missing. No automatic fallback can cross the configured ceiling. Authentication, workspace/browser permissions, separate review and exact evidence gates remain independent requirements.

Quota failover is enabled by default, independently of adaptive budgeting. When a CLI reports exhausted quota or a rate limit, ATL remembers a cooldown in .trust/manager/provider-quota.json, selects another eligible configured route, and continues the same lifecycle under the remaining session/time allowance. A failed attempt still consumes its session and appears in reports. An explicit role/model preference can be replaced for this quota recovery; turn off quota failover in Settings to prevent automatic retries.

With a configured model pool, alternatives must meet the required capability and model ceiling. Without a pool and with automatic model routing off, ATL can use only existing configured provider defaults. It does not enroll a new provider or guess new model ids. Fresh verified quota observations are preferred over unknown alternatives. Unknown quota may be tried, but is never labelled available. A provider-wide failure skips that provider across tasks; a known model-scoped failure skips only that model. Quota cooldown defaults to thirty minutes; recognized rate limits use sixty seconds. No permanent lockout is inferred when a reset time is unavailable. If every eligible alternative is unavailable, the task retains its exact blocker and cooldown time; it cannot run through a quota, permission, model ceiling or budget boundary.

Check: node verification/provider_quota_failover_test.mjs exercises a real two-task queue with an exhausted deterministic adapter and a working backup.

Plan Studio shows a resource estimate for each task card and its build, review and verification roles. Its automatic provider option also applies the pool to generation, regeneration and plan accuracy review; each call keeps the existing one-session confirmation and timeout. Built-in subscription planning uses read-only permissions. Task details and launch preview show the decision; activity records resource_budget, resource_route and resource_route_blocked.

Verification: node verification/resource_policy_test.mjs, node verification/resource_policy_ui_test.mjs, existing provider/Plan Studio and launch regression suites, and npm run ui:css:check.

Per-task provider and model

Open a task, choose Actions → Provider / model, and select a configured provider and exact model. The choice is saved on that task and used for later Rowan, Sage, and Beacon sessions. Use project / automatic route removes the task choice. A provider/model explicitly selected for a particular run takes precedence over the saved task route. Changes are refused while a queue run is active, so an in-flight session keeps its original route. The resource policy's approved model pool and capability ceiling still apply.
